DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
This review gets its arithmetic right but its conclusions wrong. The core figures (the £810 a week, the competitor midpoints, the plate counts) all check out. However, the paper misreads its own table on the risotto, and it leaves out a beef price rise that it reports itself. Together these mean the risotto recommendation should be reversed and the profit and margin projections are significantly overstated.

## 1. The risotto has the *best* margin, not the weakest

Table 1 shows the mushroom risotto at **80%**, the highest gross margin on the menu. Its cash profit per plate is £11.20 (£14.00 − £2.80), more than the burger (£10.80) and the curry (£10.90). It is also only *joint* lowest in sales, level with the specials at 90 plates.

The proposed replacement is "a seasonal vegetarian special." Specials currently run at **64%**. If the new dish performs like the existing specials at £14, profit per plate falls from £11.20 to about £8.96. Over 90 plates that is **about £200 a week, or roughly £10,500 a year, lost**, which works against the margin goal the paper is trying to reach.

The risotto also appears to be the only vegetarian main on the regular menu. Vegetarian guests often decide where a whole table books, so their custom affects more than the 90 risotto plates.

Section 5.2 and the author's summary should be withdrawn or rewritten. On these figures, the risotto is a dish to keep.

## 2. The 12% beef increase is left out of the projection

Section 4 reports that beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 ignores it. Applying 12% to the full plate cost of the two beef dishes, which slightly overstates the effect because not every ingredient on the plate is beef:

| Dish | New price | New food cost | Extra profit per plate | Weekly effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £17.50 | £5.10 | +£1.00 | +£310 |
| Beef burger | £16.00 | £4.70 (was £4.20) | +£0.50 | +£129 |
| Sirloin steak | £28.00 | £11.65 (was £10.40) | +£0.75 | +£90 |
| **Total** | | | | **about £529 a week, roughly £27,500 a year** |

This is about **£27,500 a year, not £42,000**. Two-thirds of the claimed gain comes from beef dishes, and most of it goes on the beef cost increase.

After the change, the burger's margin falls from 72% to about 71%, and the steak's from 60% to about 58%. The beef price rises mainly prevent those margins from falling further. They do not improve them.

## 3. The 71% main-course margin claim doesn't hold

Using Table 1 and leaving out the specials, whose price isn't given, the current main-course margin is **about 69.9%**:

- Revenue: £16,005 a week
- Food cost: £4,821 a week

Adding £810 of revenue and no extra cost gives about 71.3%. That is where the paper's figure comes from. With the beef increase included, it is **about 69.7%**, almost exactly where it is now. Swapping the risotto for a 64% special would push it slightly lower.

There is a broader point too. Main courses already run at roughly 70%. The fall in overall food margin from 70% to 67% must therefore come largely from **starters and desserts**, which this paper doesn't examine. Repricing mains cannot "restore our 70% overall target" if the decline is happening elsewhere.

## 4. Check whether prices include VAT

UK menu prices include VAT at 20%. The margins in Table 1 appear to be calculated on the VAT-inclusive price. For example, fish and chips works out at 69% on £16.50, but only about 63% on the £13.75 the restaurant keeps after VAT.

If that's the case:

- Every margin in the paper is overstated, including presumably the 70% target and the 67% current figure.
- Each £1.00 price rise brings in only £0.83 of revenue.
- The net weekly gain after the beef increase falls to **about £394, or roughly £20,500 a year**.

Ask the author to confirm which basis is being used.

## 5. Other problems

- **Trading days:** Section 8 says "six trading days a week." Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **"We remain the value option":** at present you are the cheapest of the six restaurants for all three dishes. At the new prices, you would no longer be cheapest for any of them:
  - fish and chips at £17.50, against £16.95 elsewhere
  - burger at £16.00, against £15.50
  - steak at £28.00, against £27.00
  
  "Below the midpoint" is true, but the positioning does change.
- **Repeat rate is not price tolerance:** a 60% repeat rate shows loyalty. It doesn't show how sensitive those guests are to price, and regulars are actually the guests most likely to notice an increase. The 2024 comparison ("no visible effect") is anecdotal unless booking data supports it.
- **Seasonality affects the monitoring:** comparing April and May against a January–February baseline mixes the price change up with the normal spring rise in trade. Volumes could look steady even if the price rise were costing covers. Compare against the same weeks of 2025 instead.
- **Some figures are asserted without data:** the share of weekday lunch trade is called "small" but never measured. Specials are averaged together, which is why their price is missing.

## What does hold up

- All the Table 1 margins are calculated correctly.
- The plate counts add up to 1,050.
- The competitor midpoints are right (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50), and all three new prices fall below them.
- The £810 and £42,120 figures are correct as calculated.
- The price rises themselves are reasonable. The problem is that the paper overstates what they achieve.

## How sensitive the gain is to volume

Once the beef increase is included, the burger and steak can each lose only about **4–5% of their volume** before their extra profit disappears. Fish and chips can lose about 8%. "If volumes hold" therefore matters more than the paper suggests.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Keep the risotto.** If the goal is to refresh the vegetarian offer, aim any new dish at a margin of at least 80%.
2. **Recalculate section 5.3** with the beef increase included, and on a VAT-exclusive basis if that applies.
3. **Restate the margin outcome** as roughly maintaining main-course margin, not raising it to 71%.
4. **Extend the review** to starters and desserts, where the overall margin decline seems to originate.
5. **Fix "six trading days"** and **change the monitoring baseline** to the same weeks of last year.

The author calls the plan "low-risk and well evidenced." The evidence is good, but the paper draws the wrong conclusions from it in two places. It does not support removing the risotto, and it does not support the headline profit figure.
